newsitem.title: USA: Great Western seeks time, alternatives.
newsitem.headline: Great Western seeks time, alternatives.

text.p: Great Western Financial Corp. sought to buy time to fend off H.F. Ahmanson and Co.'s $6.2 billion takeover bid Friday as its bankers met with potential rival suitors, sources close to Great Western said.
"Their bankers are busy and driving the process," said one banking industry source, noting a rival bid could emerge soon.
A source close to Great Western, the nation's second largest savings and loan, said "exploratory discussions" with other parties were ongoing.
Meanwhile, Great Western adopted an amendment giving its board 10 days to set a record date after receiving a request for a vote on a shareholder proposal.
Ahmanson said Tuesday it plans to solicit written consents from other shareholders on proposals related to the takeover.
Without the amendment, Ahmanson could have caused a record date to be set immediately by simply delivering a consent from one shareholder.

"The significance of that (amendment) is if Great Western's talking to other parites, it may want (time) to be able to deliver an attractive alternative to Ahmanson's proposal to shareholders," said Steve Cohen, research director and takeover specialist at Kellner, DiLeo & Co., a New York money management firm.
The amendment is meant to stop Ahmanson, the No. 1 savings and loan, from "stampeding shareholders into acting before they have all necessary information," said another source close to Great Western.
Sources said possible bidders that Great Western may have contacted include First Bank System Inc., Washington Mutual Savings Bank and Norwest Corp.
NationsBank Corp. and First Nationwide Holding Inc. were also viewed as expansion-minded banks that could afford to bid for the California savings and loan, analysts said.
All the companies declined to comment.
"Great Western has a fiduciary duty to look at options. Another bid could happen quickly," said the banking source.
But others said it may take weeks before a rival bid for Great Western, with $63 billion in assets, is worked out.

Ahmanson had no immediate comment about the amendment, although Chief Executive Officer Charles Rinehart sent a letter to Great Western's board Friday clarifying Ahmanson's plans for integration, should the merger occur.

The letter was a response to a memo circulated to Great Western employees by Chief Executive John Maher who expressed outrage at Ahmanson for saying job losses related to a merger would be targeted at Great Western employees.
Analysts estimate 2,500 jobs would be cut.
Rinehart said layoffs would be "minimal" in a merger if Great Western implemented hiring restraints.
Ahmanson has implemented a policy of hiring only as a necessity and has asked Great Western to follow suit.
But Ahmanson reiterated its commitment to its own employees and said layoffs may be higher at Great Western, even with a white knight.

"Disproportionate treatment of employees occurs -- as a reality -- in virtually every merger and would occur if Great Western were acquired by a third party, and any suggestion to the contrary is both inaccurate and creates misleading expectations for the Great Western employees," Rinehart said.
